nodes.ask: Adult with flank pain or unable to pass urine. First moves?
options: Vitals, abdomen, bladder exam, urine test, and hCG where relevant
Low-dose CT first, then examine once the stone is confirmed
Analgesia, then discharge home if the pain settles in an hour
A plain KUB film first, and a urinalysis only if a stone shows up
nodes.chainStep: Vital signs; abdominal exam for a pulsatile mass and a palpable bladder; urinalysis; urine hCG in women of reproductive age; analgesia while the workup runs
nodes.why: Flank pain is nonspecific: an abdominal aortic aneurysm, appendicitis, diverticulitis and ectopic pregnancy all mimic renal colic. The vital signs and abdomen pick out shock, a pulsatile mass and a full bladder, the urinalysis shows blood or infection, and urine hCG, checked in all women of reproductive age, decides the imaging, because in pregnancy ultrasound replaces CT. Imaging and discharge decisions come after these checks.

orders.dose: All women of reproductive age

nodes.note: Not in this version: children, kidney transplant recipients, and flank pain or hematuria after trauma.

nodes.label: Vitals, exam, urinalysis and pregnancy test

outcomes.if: Aneurysm suspected, or shock without fever; a pulsatile mass, a known aneurysm, or hypotension without fever
Septic shock; fever with hypotension, no pulsatile mass
Pregnant, location unknown; positive hCG, no scan yet showing an intrauterine pregnancy
Unable to pass urine; lower abdominal pain, fullness or a palpable bladder, no fever, pressure normal
Retention with fever, no shock; unable to pass urine with a fever, pressure normal
Infection with stone features; fever, pyuria or nitrite with colicky pain or a known stone, pressure normal
Fever and pyuria, no stone features; flank pain, pressure normal; blood in the urine alone is common in pyelonephritis
Pregnant, intrauterine pregnancy known; colicky flank pain, no fever, pressure normal
Suspected renal colic, no infection; no fever, pyuria or nitrite, not pregnant, pressure normal

nodes.summary: Flank pain with a pulsatile mass or known aneurysm, or shock without fever: continue in the abdominal pain pathway (pw_abdominal_pain), which takes shock with a mass or known aneurysm as a suspected rupture, other shock through its unstable route, and a stable painful aneurysm to CT angiography.

Septic shock with flank pain: resuscitate in the sepsis pathway (pw_sepsis_fever), whose urinary route images the kidneys at once and drains an obstructed kidney or an abscess urgently with antibiotics running; in a septic, hypotensive patient ACR rates a nephrostomy usually appropriate and a stent may be appropriate, and the stone waits until the infection is controlled.

Retention with fever, no shock: drain the bladder by urethral catheter, which suits a temporary cause such as infection; send the urine for culture, treat the infection separately, and admit for urosepsis; this route is not covered further in this version.

Positive pregnancy test with pain and no confirmed intrauterine pregnancy: continue in the abdominal pain pathway (pw_abdominal_pain), whose pregnancy route starts with a transvaginal ultrasound and hCG to find or exclude an ectopic pregnancy.

nodes.ask: Suspected renal colic, afebrile, not pregnant. Analgesia?
options: An NSAID first, for example IV ketorolac
IV morphine first; an NSAID only if it fails
Hyoscine (an antispasmodic) with an opioid
IV acetaminophen (paracetamol) first; an NSAID if it fails
nodes.chainStep: Ketorolac 30 mg IV once (15 mg if 65 or older, renally impaired or under 50 kg), or another NSAID by any route; IV acetaminophen if NSAIDs are contraindicated or not enough, then an opioid; no antispasmodic; ondansetron and IV fluids as needed
nodes.why: NICE offers an NSAID by any route first: against opioids, antispasmodics and IV acetaminophen it cut the need for rescue medication, and it reduced pain with fewer adverse effects. IV acetaminophen comes next if NSAIDs are contraindicated or not enough, an opioid only if both are, and antispasmodics are not offered. Ketorolac is the usual US parenteral NSAID, 15 to 30 mg IV or IM; IV acetaminophen matched ketorolac in one meta-analysis, but the data are too thin to prefer it.

orders.dose: IV, one dose of 30 mg under 65 years, or 15 mg if 65 or older, renally impaired or under 50 kg; repeated dosing 30 mg every 6 hours (at most 120 mg a day), or 15 mg every 6 hours (at most 60 mg a day) in those groups; IV and oral use together no more than 5 days

Advanced renal impairment or risk of renal failure from volume depletion (correct hypovolemia first); StatPearls adds pregnancy, GFR under 30 mL/min, a significant upper GI bleed, and NSAID or aspirin allergy

sources.where: Boxed warning, renal risk; Dosage and Administration

orders.item: NSAID not possible or not enough
orders.dose: IV acetaminophen next, then an opioid if both are contraindicated or not enough (NICE); US reviews give morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV or IM when ketorolac fails
Not stated in the sources read; no IV acetaminophen label was read
Do not offer
Ondansetron 4 to 8 mg IV or orally may be preferred; IV fluids for dehydration from vomiting or poor intake, not to flush out the stone

nodes.note: NICE puts IV acetaminophen before opioids; US practice and StatPearls reach for IV morphine after ketorolac. Both keep the NSAID first.

nodes.ask: Suspected renal colic, not pregnant, analgesia given. Imaging?
options: Low-dose noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast, portal phase
Intravenous urography to show the level of obstruction
MR urography without contrast, to avoid radiation
nodes.chainStep: Low-dose noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis within 24 hours; ultrasound first instead in pregnancy and in children, and acceptable in a younger adult with typical, controlled pain
nodes.why: Noncontrast CT is the reference standard for stones, with sensitivity as high as 97%, and a low-dose technique keeps that accuracy (pooled sensitivity 97%, specificity 95%); it sizes and places the stone and shows other causes of flank pain. NICE offers it within 24 hours and ACR rates it usually appropriate. IV contrast can hide stones in the collecting system, and IV urography and MR urography are rated usually not appropriate first tests. A US multispecialty consensus would skip CT in a younger patient whose typical pain is controlled, but recommends CT at about 55 without a stone history, in older patients whatever the history, and whenever the pain cannot be relieved.

sources.where: Variant 1, A and C; Variant 1 rating table

orders.dose: Urgent, within 24 hours of presentation
Pregnancy: ultrasound instead of CT. Children and young people: ultrasound first

orders.item: Ultrasound first or no CT (US consensus)
orders.dose: Younger patients (about 35) with typical, controlled pain may avoid CT even without a stone history; CT at about 55 without a stone history, and in older patients regardless; reduced-dose CT whenever CT is used, including when pain cannot be relieved

nodes.note: NICE scans every adult with suspected renal colic; the 2019 consensus panel (ACEP, ACR and AUA members) accepts ultrasound or no imaging in younger patients with typical, controlled pain. Both scan a patient of about 55 or more without a stone history, and anyone whose pain cannot be relieved.

nodes.label: Low-dose CT, creatinine and pain after analgesia

outcomes.if: Ureteric stone under 5 mm, pain controlled; likely to pass on its own

orders.dose: About 90% of stones under 5 mm pass within 4 weeks
Modest added benefit that may not justify routine use; NICE still allows one for distal stones under 10 mm

outcomes.if: Distal ureteric stone 5 to under 10 mm, pain controlled; a candidate for an alpha blocker
Proximal or mid-ureteric stone 5 to under 10 mm; pain controlled, alpha blockers not shown to help
Stone 10 mm or more, pain controlled; unlikely to pass, kidney function normal

orders.dose: Offered within 48 hours of diagnosis or readmission when the stone is unlikely to pass; 10 to 20 mm: ureteroscopy, or shockwave lithotripsy if it can clear the stone within 4 weeks
Stones over 10 mm generally need surgery; over 7 mm they are much less likely to pass

outcomes.if: Urgent urology criterion; pain or vomiting not controlled, AKI, a solitary kidney or both sides blocked
No ureteric stone; CT shows another cause, a kidney stone that does not explain the pain, or nothing

nodes.ask: Distal ureteric stone 5 to under 10 mm, pain controlled. Plan?
options: Tamsulosin daily with an NSAID, and urology follow-up
Ureteroscopy before discharge, to clear the stone at once
Nifedipine daily as the expulsive drug of choice
IV fluids to flush the stone, then discharge
nodes.chainStep: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily (off-label for stones) and an NSAID; watchful waiting; urology if not passed in 4 to 6 weeks, or sooner for fever, uncontrolled pain or worsening kidney function
nodes.why: NICE considers alpha blockers for distal ureteric stones under 10 mm (off-label), and the benefit is largest for stones of 5 to 10 mm (number needed to treat 6), with fewer pain episodes and less analgesia. Alpha blockers beat calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine. A stone this size with controlled symptoms can be managed as an outpatient with prompt follow-up and no immediate surgery, and fluids do not flush a stone out. Surgery is for failure to pass in 4 to 6 weeks, uncontrolled symptoms, infection or worsening kidney function.

sources.where: Treatment / Management, MET; Indications for Surgical Intervention

orders.dose: 0.4 mg once daily, about half an hour after the same meal each day (the labeled BPH dose; use for stones is off-label)

sources.where: 2 Dosage and Administration; 1 Indications and Usage

orders.dose: Not stated in the sources read
Less effective than alpha blockers for stone passage; not the first choice
If the stone has not passed or progressed in 4 to 6 weeks; sooner for uncontrolled symptoms, infection, a solitary kidney or worsening renal failure
Prompt outpatient follow-up for uncomplicated stones

nodes.summary: Ureteric stone likely to pass, pain controlled: home with an NSAID and watchful waiting, tamsulosin for a distal stone of 5 to under 10 mm (it adds little under 5 mm), and serum calcium measured; urology if the stone has not passed in 4 to 6 weeks, and sooner for fever, uncontrolled pain or worsening kidney function.

Proximal or mid-ureteric stone of 5 to under 10 mm, pain controlled: NICE makes no alpha blocker recommendation here and the MET review finds the benefit modest; urology review, and NICE offers treatment within 48 hours if it is unlikely to pass: shockwave lithotripsy, or ureteroscopy if lithotripsy cannot clear it within 4 weeks.

Ureteric stone of 10 mm or more with pain controlled: unlikely to pass, so NICE offers treatment within 48 hours of diagnosis: ureteroscopy for stones of 10 to 20 mm, or shockwave lithotripsy if it can clear the stone within 4 weeks.

nodes.ask: Ureteric stone with an urgent urology criterion. Next?
options: Admit, nil by mouth, and urgent urology review today
Home on tamsulosin and oral opioids; clinic in 4 weeks
Repeat the CT in 48 hours before calling urology
Admit for analgesia; urology only if a fever starts
nodes.chainStep: Admit; nil by mouth; IV analgesia and antiemetic; urgent urology review today: immediate decompression for both sides blocked, a blocked solitary kidney or kidney injury, and surgical treatment within 48 hours for pain that is not tolerated (NICE)
nodes.why: A stone in a solitary kidney, severe kidney injury and intractable pain or nausea are reasons to admit, and failure to control symptoms, uncontrollable pain, a solitary kidney, both ureters blocked, anuria or worsening renal failure are indications for surgery. NICE offers surgical treatment within 48 hours when the pain is ongoing and not tolerated or the stone is unlikely to pass, and a 2024 review lists bilateral obstruction, an obstructed solitary kidney and acute renal insufficiency among the reasons for immediate intervention to restore drainage. Keep the patient nil by mouth until surgery is ruled out; waiting for a fever or a repeat scan delays treatment that is already indicated.

sources.where: Indications for Surgical Intervention; Treatment / Management

orders.dose: Ureteric stones with ongoing pain that is not tolerated, or unlikely to pass: surgical treatment (including shockwave lithotripsy) within 48 hours of diagnosis or readmission
Until surgery is deemed unnecessary
A significant stone in a solitary kidney, severe kidney injury, an infected stone, intractable pain or nausea, extravasation or sepsis
Can promptly relieve the pain and symptoms of ureteral obstruction

sources.where: Treatment / Management, Double J stent placement

orders.dose: Immediate intervention to restore drainage for bilateral obstruction, an obstructed solitary kidney, acute renal insufficiency, high-grade obstruction or uncontrollable pain
Stent, nephrostomy or ureteroscopy: not stated in the sources read

nodes.summary: Ureteric stone with pain or vomiting that will not settle, kidney injury, a solitary kidney or both sides blocked: admit and keep nil by mouth for urgent urology review today, with immediate decompression for both sides blocked, a blocked solitary kidney or kidney injury, and surgical treatment within 48 hours for pain that is not tolerated (NICE); acute obstructive uropathy can bring renal failure or sepsis.

No ureteric stone on CT: noncontrast CT also diagnoses other causes of flank pain, from an aortic aneurysm to appendicitis and diverticulitis; treat the cause it shows, or continue in the abdominal pain pathway (pw_abdominal_pain).

nodes.ask: Infection signs, flank pain and a stone feature, pressure normal. Next?
options: Cultures, IV antibiotics, urgent imaging for obstruction
Tamsulosin and an NSAID at home; let the stone pass
Oral antibiotics at home; image if no better in 48 hours
Imaging first; antibiotics once a stone shows
nodes.chainStep: Midstream urine culture, then IV ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g once a day; urgent CT of the abdomen and pelvis (ultrasound in pregnancy) for an obstructing stone or a collection
nodes.why: Pyelonephritis that antibiotics alone will treat cannot be told from the far more dangerous obstructed, infected kidney without imaging, and a stone history, signs of sepsis or a patient who looks particularly ill, or where an obstructed kidney is otherwise suspected, are reasons to image now. A urine specimen taken before antibiotics greatly improves the yield, and the antibiotic then starts: ACR recommends antibiotics before any drainage when urosepsis is suspected, and StatPearls prefers a third generation cephalosporin at first. Home on tamsulosin, or a 48-hour wait, misses a surgical emergency.

sources.where: Introduction; Evaluation, Obstructive Pyelonephritis and Urosepsis

orders.dose: Midstream sample before the first antibiotic
CT of the abdomen and pelvis, with IV contrast or without and with it, rated usually appropriate with a stone history (unenhanced CT is more sensitive for small stones); ultrasound in pregnancy
Ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g IV once a day (a NICE first-choice IV agent); third generation cephalosporins are generally preferred at first for a suspected infected, obstructed kidney

nodes.note: ACR's flank pain criteria assume no sign of infection; fever with a stone history falls under its pyelonephritis criteria, which favour CT with contrast.

nodes.label: CT for obstruction or a collection

outcomes.if: Infected, obstructed kidney; a ureteric stone, with or without hydronephrosis

orders.dose: Fever with a 10 mm ureteric stone and no hydronephrosis: ACR rates retrograde stenting usually appropriate and medical management without decompression usually not appropriate
orders.note: The Variant 2 table rates medical management without decompression usually not appropriate, but its Variant 2 A text says that without evidence of obstruction, IV antibiotics, fluids and close clinical and imaging follow-up could be considered.

outcomes.if: Renal or perinephric abscess; a collection, no ureteric stone

orders.dose: Pyelonephritis with an abscess is a focus for source control, which may include drainage of the abscess
Size thresholds and the route are not stated in the sources read

outcomes.if: No obstruction, no collection; pyelonephritis without a blocked kidney

nodes.ask: Infection behind an obstructing ureteric stone. Next?
options: Urgent stent or nephrostomy, with IV antibiotics running
Ureteroscopy now to remove the stone and the infection
IV antibiotics alone; decompress if no better in 48 hours
Tamsulosin and IV antibiotics until the stone passes
nodes.chainStep: Urgent decompression by retrograde ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy with IV antibiotics running; culture the kidney urine; definitive stone treatment only after the infection has cleared, typically 1 to 2 weeks later
nodes.why: An infected kidney behind a stone is a surgical emergency: antibiotics alone are insufficient, and a retrograde stent or a percutaneous nephrostomy with antibiotics is first-line, done without waiting for the patient to become more stable, since a delay of more than 2 days raises mortality by about 30%. Neither route has better outcomes; a nephrostomy is preferred when the stone is hard to bypass or anesthesia is a risk. Definitive stone treatment waits until the infection is controlled, typically 1 to 2 weeks, so ureteroscopy now and tamsulosin while the kidney stays blocked are both wrong.

sources.where: Variant 5, A, B and E; Variant 2 rating table

orders.dose: Retrograde ureteric (double J) stent or percutaneous nephrostomy; efficacy outcomes did not differ in a 2024 meta-analysis

Nephrostomy for a stone burden hard to bypass cystoscopically or a patient who cannot tolerate anesthesia; stenting avoided when bladder access is difficult; nephrostomy contraindicated with uncorrected coagulopathy or platelet dysfunction
ACR rates a percutaneous nephrostomy usually appropriate and a retrograde stent may be appropriate
Nephrostomy urine can identify the pathogen and change the antibiotic
Postponed until the infection is controlled and the patient has fully recovered, typically 1 to 2 weeks

nodes.summary: Infected, obstructed kidney: cultures, IV antibiotics and urgent decompression by stent or nephrostomy without waiting for the patient to settle; the stone is treated once the infection is controlled, typically 1 to 2 weeks later.

Renal or perinephric abscess: admit for IV antibiotics; it is a focus for source control, so urology or interventional radiology decide on drainage; size thresholds for drainage are not in the sources read.

nodes.ask: Fever, flank pain and pyuria, no stone features. First?
options: Urine culture before antibiotics; image only if high risk
CT with contrast first for an abscess, then antibiotics
No culture; a 3-day course as for simple cystitis
Blood cultures before antibiotics; no urine culture needed
nodes.chainStep: Midstream urine culture before antibiotics; no routine imaging in a first, uncomplicated pyelonephritis; decide home or hospital
nodes.why: Send a midstream urine culture before the first antibiotic: it greatly improves the yield. Blood cultures are often sent but rarely change treatment; the urine culture is the one that decides the switch. Imaging is not beneficial in a first, uncomplicated pyelonephritis, since nearly all are afebrile by 72 hours; it is kept for high-risk patients, such as those with diabetes, immune compromise, a stone history, pregnancy or no response. More than 95% of uncomplicated patients can be treated at home on oral antibiotics, and NICE courses run 7 to 14 days by agent, not a cystitis course.

outcomes.if: Mild, drinking, not pregnant; no sepsis, vomiting or high-risk feature
Needs admission; vomiting, unable to take oral drugs, or high risk

orders.dose: Signs of sepsis, high fever, difficult pain, persistent nausea, marked debility, failed outpatient treatment, significant comorbidities, likely non-compliance or poor home care

outcomes.if: Pregnant; pyelonephritis in pregnancy

nodes.ask: Mild pyelonephritis, not pregnant, going home. Antibiotic?
options: An oral agent by local resistance, switched by culture
Nitrofurantoin for 5 days, the same as for cystitis
Fosfomycin as a single oral dose, as for cystitis
TMP-SMX twice daily now, before the culture result is known
nodes.chainStep: Oral antibiotic by local resistance, switched by the culture: ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice a day for 7 days (StatPearls: 14 days in men) where fluoroquinolone resistance is 10% or less (one IV dose of ceftriaxone first if it is higher); NICE first choice cephalexin (cefalexin) 500 mg two or three times a day for 7 to 10 days; return if not better in 48 hours
nodes.why: Give an oral antibiotic when the patient can take it, chosen by local resistance and switched by the culture. In the US a fluoroquinolone is preferred where community resistance is 10% or less, for 7 days; where resistance is higher, a long-acting parenteral dose such as ceftriaxone goes first, before discharge. NICE starts with cephalexin and keeps ciprofloxacin for when the others are unsuitable. Growing resistance makes TMP-SMX less useful empirically, so it waits for susceptibility; nitrofurantoin is not indicated for pyelonephritis, fosfomycin is not recommended for it in the US, and the 3 to 5 day courses that treat cystitis are too short.

orders.dose: 500 mg twice a day for 7 days (NICE); the label gives 250 to 500 mg every 12 hours for 7 to 14 days; US use where fluoroquinolone resistance is 10% or less

sources.where: 2 Dosage and Administration, Table 1 adult dosage

orders.dose: An initial long-acting parenteral dose (ceftriaxone, an aminoglycoside or ertapenem) in the emergency department before discharge
500 mg two or three times a day (up to 1 to 1.5 g three or four times a day if severe) for 7 to 10 days
One double-strength tablet (800/160 mg) every 12 hours; 14 days in StatPearls, 10 to 14 days on the label
Not indicated for pyelonephritis
Seek help if symptoms worsen, do not start to improve within 48 hours, or the person becomes very unwell

nodes.note: NICE NG111 makes cephalexin first choice and restricts fluoroquinolones under MHRA advice; US teaching gives an oral fluoroquinolone first where resistance allows. The IDSA 2010 guideline behind the US regimen was not read: its publisher copy was not openly accessible.

nodes.summary: Mild pyelonephritis: urine culture, an oral antibiotic chosen by local resistance and switched by the culture, and review if it is not better within 48 hours; symptoms that persist to 72 hours need imaging.

nodes.ask: Pyelonephritis needing admission, not pregnant. Empiric IV antibiotic?
options: IV ceftriaxone, narrowed by the culture
IV vancomycin alone, to cover MRSA
IV meropenem with vancomycin for broad cover
Oral ciprofloxacin, started once the vomiting settles
nodes.chainStep: Urine culture, then IV ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g once a day, narrowed by susceptibility; review by 48 hours and step down to oral when improving
nodes.why: Ceftriaxone is a good initial empiric IV choice and one of NICE's first-choice IV agents, narrowed by susceptibility. E. coli causes more than 90% of pyelonephritis in young healthy women, so vancomycin alone misses it; vancomycin or linezolid are added only when a Gram-positive organism is suspected. Carbapenems are reserved for the critically ill or when nothing else fits. Vomiting means IV treatment now: NICE gives first-choice IV antibiotics to a patient who is vomiting, unable to take oral antibiotics or severely unwell.

orders.dose: 1 to 2 g IV once a day
Initially 5 to 7 mg/kg once a day, then adjusted by serum levels, with renal monitoring
IV antibiotics reviewed by 48 hours, stepping down to oral where possible

outcomes.if: Improving; afebrile and eating by 48 to 72 hours, culture back
Still febrile at 72 hours; no response on the right antibiotic

nodes.summary: Pyelonephritis improving on IV antibiotics: step down to an oral agent chosen by the culture by 48 hours; the course length depends on the agent (NICE: ciprofloxacin 7 days, cephalexin 7 to 10 days, trimethoprim 14 days).

nodes.ask: Pyelonephritis, still febrile at 72 hours on IV antibiotics. Next?
options: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
Add a second antibiotic and wait another 72 hours
DMSA renal scan to confirm the pyelonephritis
Repeat the urine culture and continue unchanged
nodes.chainStep: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast for an abscess, obstruction or emphysematous pyelonephritis; keep IV antibiotics and change them by the culture; urology if obstructed, infectious disease advice if not
nodes.why: Nearly all uncomplicated pyelonephritis is afebrile by 72 hours, so persistent fever is a lack of response. ACR rates contrast CT usually appropriate for that complicated patient: it shows a renal or perirenal abscess, emphysematous pyelonephritis, hydronephrosis or an obstructing stone. Change the antibiotic if needed and keep it IV, but image rather than wait; a DMSA scan cannot show stones. Urology follows an obstruction, infectious disease advice a negative scan.

sources.where: Variant 1, A; Variant 2 rating table; Variant 2, A; Variant 3, D

orders.dose: Urology if imaging shows obstruction; infectious disease advice if it is negative; change the antibiotic and keep it parenteral as needed

nodes.summary: Pyelonephritis not responding at 72 hours: contrast CT; drainage of an obstruction or a collection, and infectious disease advice with a culture-guided change if the CT is negative.

options: Admit; IV cephalosporin after the urine culture
Oral ciprofloxacin at home, with review in 48 hours
Oral nitrofurantoin for 7 days at home
Low-dose CT first, to rule out an obstructing stone
nodes.chainStep: Admit; urine culture; IV cephalosporin (NICE: cefuroxime 750 mg to 1.5 g three or four times a day; US practice: ceftriaxone 1 g every 24 hours); ultrasound if imaging is needed; oral step-down after 48 hours once stable, 7 to 14 days in all; no fluoroquinolone or nitrofurantoin
nodes.why: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy is serious and usually needs hospital: StatPearls ties it to preterm labour, and NICE considers referral or specialist advice in pregnancy. A second or third generation cephalosporin is the usual first IV treatment after a urine culture (NICE first choice IV cefuroxime; ceftriaxone in US practice). Fluoroquinolones, nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin are avoided; nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin do not reach the kidney. If imaging is needed, ultrasound comes first: CT is not supported as the initial test in pregnancy.

orders.dose: 750 mg to 1.5 g three or four times a day
1 g IV every 24 hours (StatPearls review); the label range is 1 to 2 g once a day
After at least 48 hours once stable and eating; 7 to 14 days of IV and oral treatment in total
Avoid for pyelonephritis in pregnancy
Avoid from about 30 weeks; between about 20 and 30 weeks, only the lowest dose for the shortest time
Ultrasound first if imaging is needed; CT is not supported as the initial imaging in pregnancy

nodes.note: ACOG is barred, so the US regimen comes from the StatPearls review; NICE's first-choice IV agent in pregnancy is cefuroxime.

nodes.summary: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy: admit, urine culture, an IV cephalosporin, ultrasound rather than CT if imaging is needed, oral step-down after 48 hours once stable, and 7 to 14 days in total.

nodes.ask: Unable to pass urine, lower abdominal pain or fullness. First?
options: Bladder scan if unsure; catheter at once if obvious
Tamsulosin, then wait 2 hours for spontaneous voiding
CT of the abdomen and pelvis before any catheter
Suprapubic catheter as the first route of drainage
nodes.chainStep: Bedside bladder scan, without delaying catheterisation when retention is obvious; urinalysis and culture if appropriate
nodes.why: A bladder scan identifies retention, but it must not delay the catheter when retention is obvious. Over 400 mL typically means retention; under 200 mL, acute retention is unlikely and another cause is looked for. NICE catheterises men with acute retention immediately; a suprapubic tube is for a bladder that cannot be reached through the urethra or after recent prostate or urethral surgery. An alpha blocker needs about 72 hours for full effect, so waiting on it leaves the bladder full.

sources.where: Evaluation; Treatment / Management; Medical Therapy, Alpha-blockers

outcomes.if: Retention; over 400 mL, or 200 to 400 mL and the picture fits
Not retention; under 200 mL in the bladder

nodes.summary: Under 200 mL on the bladder scan: acute retention is unlikely; look for another cause of the pain or the voiding trouble, such as the urinary infection a nitrite-positive sample suggests; send it for culture.

options: Urethral catheter, draining the bladder fully at once
Drain 500 mL, clamp it, then release the rest slowly over hours
One in-and-out catheter, then home to void as usual
A suprapubic catheter first, to spare the urethra
nodes.chainStep: 16 French urethral Foley catheter, draining the bladder fully at once; a large three-way catheter instead if the urine is bloody or clots are seen; record the volume and leave the catheter in if over 400 mL; watch for post-obstructive diuresis if over 1500 mL; no prophylactic antibiotics
nodes.why: NICE catheterises men with acute retention immediately. A 16 French Foley is the usual first catheter, and rapid, complete drainage is best even for very large volumes: clamping or partial drainage does not reduce hematuria, hypotension or post-obstructive diuresis. Over 400 mL, the catheter stays in; when the bladder is merely emptied and the catheter withdrawn at once, retention returns in about half within a week. A suprapubic tube is for when the urethra cannot be passed or after recent urological surgery.

orders.dose: 16 French Foley with a 5 to 10 mL balloon; a coude tip if a standard catheter will not pass; suprapubic if the urethra cannot be passed, or after radical prostatectomy or urethral reconstruction

nodes.ask: Retention from an enlarged prostate, catheter in. Before the trial without catheter?
options: Tamsulosin now; trial without catheter in 2 to 7 days
Start finasteride and remove the catheter tomorrow
Remove the catheter today, without an alpha blocker
Book a TURP this admission, before any trial of voiding
nodes.chainStep: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily from now; trial without catheter after 2 to 7 days; urology referral; surgery only if symptoms are severe or drug treatment fails
nodes.why: NICE offers an alpha blocker before the catheter comes out. With BPH as the likely cause it makes the trial without catheter more likely to succeed and lowers the risk of recurrent retention, though about 40% still fail; it needs about 72 hours for full effect, so it starts when the catheter goes in, and the trial usually follows after 2 to 7 days. Finasteride and dutasteride need at least 6 months, and NICE keeps surgery for severe symptoms or failed drug and conservative treatment.

orders.dose: 0.4 mg once daily, about half an hour after the same meal each day
Usually after 2 to 7 days (the best timing is not established); failure is no voiding or a residual over 400 mL, success a residual under 200 mL
At least 6 months for optimal effect, so no use as a bridge to the trial without catheter
Specialist assessment for LUTS complicated by retention

nodes.summary: Acute retention from an enlarged prostate: catheterise at once, start an alpha blocker, and try without the catheter after 2 to 7 days; about 40% still fail, urology follows up, and surgery is for severe symptoms or failed drug treatment.

Retention with a drug or bowel trigger: drain the bladder, stop the drug (anticholinergics, decongestants, opioids and others), treat the cause such as constipation, offer an alpha blocker before the catheter comes out (NICE), and try without the catheter early, within hours to 3 days.
Retention with no prostate, drug, neurological or clot cause, or in a woman: not covered in this version; keep the catheter in, culture the urine and refer to urology.

Retention with back pain, saddle numbness, leg weakness or bowel change: suspect cauda equina syndrome, which MRI diagnoses; continue in the back pain pathway (pw_back_pain), which takes it to an emergency MRI. The catheter stays in.

nodes.ask: The catheter drains blood and clots, then blocks. Next?
options: Large three-way catheter, clot washout, then irrigation
Remove the catheter and let the clots pass on their own
CT urogram now, before the bladder is drained again
A smaller catheter, which passes more easily
nodes.chainStep: Large three-way urethral catheter (22 French or more), bladder washout and continuous irrigation; urology; then CT or MR urography and cystoscopy for the visible hematuria
nodes.why: Clot retention needs a large three-way catheter, 22 French or more, with continuous bladder irrigation through its extra port; clots may need evacuating by vigorous hand irrigation, and anticoagulants are stopped or reversed where possible. Irrigating blood and clots from the bladder is one of the reasons to catheterise, and a larger catheter is the exception kept for bleeding. The bladder is drained first. Afterwards, visible hematuria needs a full urological workup, because up to 30 to 40% is associated with malignancy: CT or MR urography and, in many patients, cystoscopy.

orders.dose: 22 French or larger three-way catheter; evacuate clots by hand irrigation, then continuous bladder irrigation; stop or reverse anticoagulants where possible
Not stated in the sources read
CT urography or MR urography (usually appropriate for gross hematuria) and, in many patients, cystoscopy

nodes.summary: Clot retention: a large three-way catheter, washout and continuous irrigation, then a full workup of the visible hematuria with CT or MR urography and cystoscopy, because up to 30 to 40% is associated with malignancy.

nodes.ask: Pregnant, colicky flank pain, no fever. Imaging?
options: Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder
Low-dose noncontrast CT, the most accurate test
A plain abdominal x-ray to look for the stone
MR urography with gadolinium first
nodes.chainStep: Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder; noncontrast MR urography or low-dose CT only if it is inconclusive; obstetric follow-up; no NSAID from about 30 weeks
nodes.why: In pregnancy NICE offers ultrasound instead of CT, and ACR rates kidney and bladder ultrasound usually appropriate; noncontrast MR urography or low-dose CT may be appropriate when it does not settle the question. Hydronephrosis is common in pregnancy anyway (over 80%, more often on the right, from the second trimester), so dilatation alone does not prove a stone. A plain film and gadolinium MR urography are rated usually not appropriate.

orders.dose: Noncontrast MR urography or low-dose noncontrast CT may be appropriate

The agent and dose are not stated in the sources read
Close obstetric follow-up; admission for renal colic carries up to twice the risk of preterm labour

outcomes.if: Stone seen; a ureteric stone with hydronephrosis, no fever
No stone seen; normal, or hydronephrosis without a stone

nodes.summary: Ureteric stone in pregnancy without infection: obstetric and urology care; rest, hydration, antiemetics and analgesia succeed in 70 to 80%, a stent or nephrostomy is rated usually appropriate once fever comes with hydronephrosis, and the main risk of a stone is preterm labour.

No stone on ultrasound in pregnancy: mild hydronephrosis alone may be the physiological hydronephrosis of pregnancy; if the pain persists, noncontrast MR urography or low-dose CT may be appropriate, and pregnancy causes such as preterm labour or placental abruption are considered.
